title: Stereoelectronics and conformation
goal: Predict which bond forms or breaks from how orbitals line up: anti-periplanar bonds, the Bürgi–Dunitz angle, Baldwin's rules and the anomeric effect.

problemSets.title: Anti-periplanar
problemSets.conceptInOneLine: A bond breaks best when the pair pushing it out lies anti-periplanar to it; on a ring that means axial.
problemSets.conceptCard:
Electrons flow from a filled orbital into an empty σ* orbital best when the two are **anti-periplanar**: in one plane, on opposite sides of the bond.

- **E2 on a cyclohexane**: the C–H and C–leaving group bonds must both be **axial**. A hydrogen that cannot become axial cannot leave, whatever Zaitsev's rule says
- **Epoxide opening on a locked ring**: the nucleophile attacks anti to the C–O bond and the ring moves straight into a chair with both new groups axial: **trans-diaxial** opening (the Fürst–Plattner rule). The other carbon would have to react through a twist-boat

A tert-butyl group is the usual way to **lock** a cyclohexane: it is always equatorial.

The app does not check stereochemistry yet: the structures show which atoms are bonded, and the stereochemical outcome is explained in the text.

setItems.whyThisOne: The only anti-periplanar hydrogen gives the less substituted alkene.
Two secondary carbons, one chair: the trans-diaxial rule picks the carbon.

problemSets.title: Addition to carbonyls
problemSets.conceptInOneLine: Nucleophiles reach C=O at about 107°, and what they pass on the way decides the face.
problemSets.conceptCard:
A nucleophile attacks the π* orbital of C=O along the **Bürgi–Dunitz trajectory**, about **107°** to the C=O bond, not at 90°. What lies along that path decides which face it attacks:

- **Felkin–Anh**: next to a stereocentre, put the *largest* group perpendicular to the C=O and let the nucleophile come in anti to it, past the *smallest* group
- **Cyclohexanones**: small hydrides (LiAlH₄, NaBH₄) attack **axially** and give the equatorial alcohol; bulky ones (L-Selectride) attack equatorially and give the axial alcohol

The arrows are the same as in any carbonyl addition: the selectivity is all in the approach.

The app does not check stereochemistry yet: the structures show which atoms are bonded, and the stereochemical outcome is explained in the text.

setItems.whyThisOne: A stereocentre next to C=O: which face does the Grignard reagent choose?
A locked cyclohexanone: hydride comes in axially.

problemSets.title: Ring closure
problemSets.conceptInOneLine: Baldwin's rules: a ring closes when the nucleophile can reach the right orbital at the right angle.
problemSets.conceptCard:
**Baldwin's rules** name a ring closure by three things:

1. the **ring size** formed (3, 4, 5, 6, 7)
2. **exo** if the bond that breaks ends up outside the new ring, **endo** if inside
3. the carbon attacked: **tet** (sp³, SN2), **trig** (sp², C=O or C=C), **dig** (sp, alkyne)

**5-exo-tet** and **5-exo-trig** are favoured: the nucleophile reaches 180° behind a C–X bond, or 107° to a π bond. **5-endo-trig** is *disfavoured*: from inside a five-membered ring the nucleophile cannot get to the π* orbital at the right angle, so such closures are slow or do not happen at all.

Five-membered rings close fastest of all except three: the chain loses little freedom and the ring has almost no strain.

setItems.whyThisOne: 5-exo-tet: an alkoxide displaces bromide in its own chain.
5-exo-trig at a C=C: an intramolecular oxa-Michael addition.
5-exo-trig at a C=O: a hydroxy ester closes to a lactone.
6-exo-trig: a hydroxy aldehyde closes to a six-membered hemiacetal.

problemSets.title: Anomeric effect
problemSets.conceptInOneLine: A ring oxygen lone pair anti-periplanar to a C–O bond holds OR axial and pushes leaving groups out.
problemSets.conceptCard:
In a tetrahydropyran with an OR group on the carbon next to the ring oxygen (the **anomeric carbon**), OR prefers to be **axial**, against what sterics predict. This is the **anomeric effect**: only when OR is axial does a lone pair of the ring oxygen lie anti-periplanar to the C–OR bond and feed into its σ* orbital (n → σ*).

The same overlap explains how **glycosides are hydrolysed**: once the OR oxygen is protonated, the ring oxygen pushes it out and an **oxocarbenium ion** forms. Water adds, and the acetal becomes a hemiacetal, which opens to the hydroxy aldehyde.

The app does not check stereochemistry yet: the structures show which atoms are bonded, and the stereochemical outcome is explained in the text.

setItems.whyThisOne: The ring oxygen pushes methanol out: an oxocarbenium ion, then water.

problemSets.title: Checkpoint
problemSets.conceptInOneLine: Which orbitals line up, and so which bond forms or breaks?
problemSets.conceptCard: Reactions from every set, shuffled, names hidden until you finish. Three attempts per step.

setItems.whyThisOne: Which ring size, and which carbon?
